source_document: A bounded queue stores pending work up to a fixed capacity. When the queue is full, backpressure makes producers wait instead of creating more queued work. Consumers remove queued work when they have capacity. Backpressure limits pending work; it does not make consumers process faster.
prior_answer:
1. A bounded queue holds pending work up to a fixed capacity. [SOURCE_1bcb7afa6ce2c84cba2e827b]
2. Backpressure makes producers wait when the queue is full; it does not make consumers faster. [SOURCE_1bcb7afa6ce2c84cba2e827b]
question: Explain the second point again with a simple everyday analogy.

rows.answer:
The second point is: "Backpressure makes producers wait when the queue is full; it does not make consumers faster."

Think of it like a restaurant with a limited number of tables. When the restaurant is full, the waiters (producers) can't take any more orders (work) because the tables (queue capacity) are already full. They can't just magically create more tables to seat more customers. Instead, they have to wait for an available table to process the next order. This is like backpressure - the producers wait because the queue is full, not because the consumers (customers) are suddenly able to process more orders faster.

The second point is: "Backpressure makes producers wait when the queue is full; it does not make consumers faster."

Think of it like a restaurant with a limited number of tables. When the restaurant is full, the waiters (producers) can't take in more customers (queued work) because the tables are already full. They can't just magically create more tables to seat more customers. Instead, they have to wait for an available table to become free before they can take in more customers.
